name: One for the World (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Moves money: each recipient its donors give to, read live, brings its own countries.
summary: One for the World asks students and young professionals in the US, UK, Canada and Australia to give 1% of their income to charities GiveWell recommends, through chapters at universities and graduate schools and talks at companies; this model covers its year to June 2024 ($758K of its own costs across its US company and UK charity; donors' money passed on is left out). At the defaults it averts about 6.4 years of healthy life per $1,000: of the $1.55M its donors gave that year, its own count says it caused 44%; most of that is the yearly giving of people who pledged in earlier years, so the year is credited with its 166 new pledges' discounted lifetime giving plus its one-off gifts, about $350K in all, each dollar valued at its donors' charities (84% to GiveWell's recommended charities), half counted as new money, the next dollar at 57% of the past average. It is more than ten times its peers because the money it moves goes almost all to top global-health charities: it sits above the charities it funds, not among typical global-health programmes; it is far below Giving What We Can and Effektiv Spenden because it causes under half a dollar of discounted giving per dollar it spends. The result moves most with the discount rate, its next-dollar figure, its own count of what it caused and how this year's pledges compare with earlier years'; no branch is discounted for missing data, since money moved is counted.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

source.note: Its 'total money moved', including the small share to charities outside GiveWell's list. Of it, $1,303,670 went to GiveWell's recommended charities (2023-2024 Impact Report, p. 18).

rows.explainer: Donations by its pledgers and other donors in its 2023-2024 year through its platform, workplace giving (Benevity) and the off-platform giving it could trace, rounded in the source (hence the range); its UK charity's giving (£159K, its trustees' report) is taken as included, since the report covers chapters in the US, UK, Canada and Australia. Most of it is the yearly giving of people who pledged in earlier years: converted to a flow below.

rows.label: Unrecorded giving: money moved it doesn't see, as a multiple
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on its own statement a year later that it is 'likely missing six figures worth of money moved a year' from off-platform giving (EA Forum, November 2025): $100K or more on about $1.5M, so 7% (0 to 20%). Its 2023-2024 count already includes the off-platform donors it could confirm, by a stricter method (Impact Report p. 20).

rows.label: Share of its donors' giving that happens only because of One for the World

source.title: One for the World, 2023-2024 Impact Report
source.quote: Move $1.1m in counterfactual donations to GiveWell nonprofits ... $1,107,000 $575,956*
source.note: $575,956 of $1,303,670 moved to GiveWell's charities: 44.2%. Donors are asked at checkout whether they knew GiveWell before; its largest donors and corporate donors were assessed one by one. Its 2021-2022 method gave 68% ('68% of our donors noted that they were not familiar with GiveWell'), and its 2023-2024 target implied 61% ($1.1M of $1.8M).

rows.explainer: Its own effect (the shared rule, facts/meta.json own_effect_share: the organisation's own donor survey where it has one; it handles its non-respondents itself). The rest its donors would have given to GiveWell's charities anyway. 44% by its newer, stricter method, which it calls 'less of an estimate of our actual counterfactuality and more a measure of what portion of money moved we have high confidence is counterfactual'. Low: the shared figure for an organisation without a survey (30%); high: the share its target implied (61%), below its older method's 68%, which ignored that its largest donors are less often counterfactual.

rows.label: Giving in the year that it caused (US$)
rows.explainer: The year's money moved, with unrecorded giving, net of what donors would have given to GiveWell's charities anyway: about $734K.

rows.label: Share of the year's money moved that is pledgers' recurring giving
rows.explainer: Our judgment: its 1% Pledge is recurring giving (its model is 'pledging now, donating later', activating pledges recruited up to 4 years earlier, 2021-2022 report), and most of its money is pledgers' monthly gifts. One-off gifts are the rest: corporate one-off donations were $82,922 (Impact Report p. 18), and giving-season and workplace one-off gifts add more ($335,831 came from corporate workplaces, one-time and Benevity donors together, p. 13). 80% (60 to 95%).

rows.label: Years a new pledger can keep giving
rows.explainer: Our judgment: its pledgers are students and young professionals, most in their twenties, who pledge 1% of their income for their working lives; from about 27 to 65 is 38 years. Low: a shorter giving life, as for Giving What We Can's 25; high: from 22. The shared persistence curve below decides how many still give.

rows.label: Discounted years of giving per new pledge (share still giving each year, summed)
rows.explainer: The shared pledge-persistence figures (facts/meta.json, from Giving What We Can's cohort data): the share of pledgers giving in year t is floor + (first year − floor) × (1 − decay)^t, each year discounted at the site's rate. Its own figures look alike in the early years: it kept 80% of active donors' yearly giving in 2022-2023 (2022-2023 report) and lost 'over 20%' of pledges in 2023-2024; the curve keeps 75-82% from year to year in years 2 and 3.

rows.label: Undiscounted years of giving per new pledge, on the same curve
rows.explainer: The same shared curve summed without discounting: the years of giving one cohort adds to the yearly flows of all later years.

rows.label: Years from a pledge to its first gift
rows.explainer: Our judgment: most of its 2023-2024 pledges came from undergraduate chapters (117 of 166, Impact Report p. 22), who pledge 1% of post-graduation income and start giving when they graduate, up to four years later ('we are constantly activating pledges that were recruited up to 4 years ago', 2021-2022 report); graduate and corporate pledgers give at once. About a year on average (a quarter to two and a half).

rows.label: The year's new pledges' lifetime giving against the average cohort behind the year's recurring giving
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The recurring giving of a year comes from pledges made over many years; this year's spending is credited only with this year's pledges, so the year's flow is scaled to this year's cohort. It made 166 pledges in 2023-2024 (p. 22) against about 320 a year on average before (2,913 pledgers in nine years by 2023, 2022-2023 report), and says the 'decline is more significant than the drop in money moved'; but 'newer pledges are giving more' (graduate and MBA pledgers). 166/320 = 0.52, times about 1.25 for the larger pledges: 0.65. Low: the count alone, less for the over 20% of pledges withdrawn; high: as large as the average cohort.

rows.label: A year's recurring giving to the discounted lifetime giving of the year's new pledges
rows.explainer: Pledges are a flow (docs/normalization.md 2.8, Convention 3): a year's spending earns its new pledges' discounted lifetime giving. In a steady state a year's recurring giving equals one cohort's undiscounted lifetime giving, so the year's flow × discounted ÷ undiscounted years (about 0.56 at 4%), after the wait to the first gift, × this cohort against the average one, is the new pledges' value. About 0.35.

rows.label: Lifetime giving it caused through the year's new pledges, discounted (US$)
rows.explainer: The recurring part of the year's caused giving, converted to the discounted lifetime giving of this year's pledges.

rows.label: One-off giving it caused in the year (US$)
rows.explainer: One-off gifts are a flow already: the year's, against the year's cost.

rows.label: Money moved that it caused (US$)
rows.explainer: This year's pledges' discounted lifetime giving and the year's one-off gifts, net of what donors would have given to GiveWell's charities anyway: about $360K. Where it went is in value_destinations; half of it counts as new money, the rest only for the gain over where it would have gone (the shared rows).

rows.label: Money moved it caused per dollar of its own costs
rows.explainer: Context: about 0.5 dollars of caused, discounted giving per dollar it spends; its gross yearly ratio of money moved to own costs is about 2.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium, Helen Keller Intl, New Incentives), each at GiveWell's figure for the charity on the rankings (its programmes and locations weighted by funding) under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: Valued by where this organisation's money went: its own published split, each recipient at its live result on this site (value_destinations).

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.label: Share of money moved that is new money
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to the charities One for the World's donors gave to (its 2023-2024 split, live), units of value
rows.explainer: Where its donors' money went in 2023-2024, each recipient at its figure on the rankings under your values, by the site's rule for a split (normalization.md 2.8). 84% went to charities GiveWell recommends (its 'effective money moved', $1.30M of $1.55M); split as the donations through its own books were (Form 990 Schedule I): $495,387 to GiveWell for its recommended charities and $10,217 through Every.org to them, both at GiveWell's Top Charities (value_global_health), and $162,953 to Against Malaria Foundation at its figure. Gifts made off its books follow the same portfolio (Malaria Consortium, Against Malaria Foundation, Helen Keller Intl, New Incentives and GiveWell's All Grants Fund), so they take the same split. The other 16% went to charities outside GiveWell's list, mostly GiveDirectly, the one it names (Impact Report p. 19), at GiveDirectly's figure.

rows.label: Value per unit affected per year, in units of value
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so this row multiplies nothing. It keeps the template's figure and range (a typical policy win's value and chance from the family's reference classes) only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

Expected value of the policy or research (before adjustments)
Side effects of the money moved, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: Good and harm beyond the donations counted: chapter leaders and pledgers who go on to give more, take Giving What We Can's 10% Pledge or move into effective-giving work (its chief operating officer's own path), and talks that lead people to give to GiveWell's charities directly (positive); a 1% norm that anchors some who would have given more, and volunteers' and donors' attention drawn from other good uses (negative). 5% (−5% to +20%) of the modelled value, our judgment, as for Giving What We Can's model, whose pledge work is the closest reference.

rows.label: Value of the money moved (units of value)
rows.explainer: Money moved × the net value of a dollar moved, with the side effects.

How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.explainer: One for the World's own figure (facts/next_dollar.json): 57% (29–95%). Money is the constraint (about four months of unrestricted reserves in June 2025, a projected $160K deficit for 2025-2026, Open Philanthropy's operating support ended), but the next dollar funds a growth strategy whose early results are mixed, at an organisation that missed most of its own targets in 2022-2024.
